question:
For an all-or-nothing vaccine, will the 1-incidence rate ratio overestimate / underestimate / correctly estimate the per-exposure vaccine efficacy?

Answer Choices:
A. overestimate
B. underestimate
C. correctly estimate
D. /
E. /

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: B. underestimate

For an all-or-nothing vaccine the 1-incidence rate ratio will tend to underestimate the per-exposure efficacy. In an all-or-nothing setting a fraction of vaccinees are completely protected while the remainder experience the same hazard as unvaccinated individuals. Because the incidence rate ratio averages over the whole population (including the fully protected subset), the observed reduction in incidence is diluted relative to the protection actually conferred on each exposure that a susceptible vaccinated person faces. Consequently the quantity 1-IRR lies below the true per-exposure efficacy; the bias grows with the proportion of the population that is fully protected and with longer follow-up, both of which increase the weight of the zero-event group in the overall rate.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction \(p\) of recipients are fully protected (0 hazard) and the remainder \(1-p\) are completely unprotected (hazard \(\lambda\)). The unvaccinated group has hazard \(\lambda\) throughout. At \(t=0\) the observed incidence rate ratio equals \(1-p\), so \(1-\text{IRR}=p\). As follow-up continues, infections remove only unprotected individuals from the vaccinated cohort; the vaccinated person-time denominator therefore contains an ever-larger fraction of permanently immune people who contribute zero events. Consequently the observed rate in the vaccinated arm falls faster than the true unprotected fraction would predict, driving IRR below \(1-p\) and \(1-\text{IRR}\) above \(p\). The 1-incidence-rate-ratio therefore overestimates the per-exposure (all-or-nothing) efficacy.  
Answer: A

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing vaccine (complete protection for a fraction of recipients, zero for the rest), the force of infection among the vaccinated is always scaled by exactly the unprotected fraction. This produces a constant hazard ratio equal to that fraction. Consequently the observed incidence rate ratio exactly recovers the proportion protected, which is the relevant per-exposure efficacy parameter. No systematic bias arises from differential depletion or time-varying hazards. The answer is therefore C.

(The result is model-independent under standard assumptions of exchangeable exposures and no waning.)

5.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing vaccine the 1-incidence rate ratio should underestimate the per-exposure vaccine efficacy. In the all-or-nothing setting a fraction of vaccinated individuals receive complete protection while the rest behave exactly like unvaccinated controls; the observed incidence rate in the vaccinated arm is therefore an average of two very different subgroups. Because the rate ratio mixes the fully protected and fully susceptible individuals, the reduction it registers is smaller than the protection that actually occurs on each exposure for the protected subgroup. Consequently the quantity 1-IRR lies below the true per-exposure efficacy, producing an underestimate rather than an overestimate or an exact match. This dilution effect is specific to the all-or-nothing mechanism and does not appear when protection is applied uniformly on every exposure.

12.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing vaccine the incidence rate ratio should correctly estimate per-exposure vaccine efficacy. Because protection is binary (full or none) rather than fractional per exposure, the ratio of cumulative incidences directly recovers the proportion of individuals who are fully protected; that proportion is exactly the per-exposure efficacy parameter under the all-or-nothing model. In contrast, a leaky vaccine would produce a different bias because partial protection compounds over repeated exposures. Hence the answer is C.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing vaccine, a fraction of vaccinated individuals are fully protected (VE=100% against infection per exposure) while the remainder receive no protection. The observed incidence rate in the vaccinated group is therefore driven solely by the unprotected fraction and equals (1 - p) * λ, where p is the protected fraction and λ is the incidence rate among the unvaccinated. Consequently the incidence-rate ratio equals exactly 1 - p, so 1 - IRR recovers p without bias. This quantity is also the average per-exposure efficacy, hence the IRR-based estimator is unbiased (C).

(The contrast with leaky vaccines arises because the latter produce differential depletion of susceptibles over time, which distorts the observed rate ratio away from the constant per-exposure protection parameter; that distortion is absent under the all-or-nothing mechanism.)

11.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing vaccine (complete protection in a fraction of recipients, zero protection in the rest), the incidence rate among the vaccinated equals (1-p) times the unvaccinated incidence, where p is the proportion fully protected. Thus IRR = 1-p exactly, so 1-IRR recovers p. Because protection is absolute on every exposure for the protected fraction, this value is also the per-exposure efficacy. The 1-IRR therefore correctly estimates per-exposure VE (choice C).

(The contrast case is a leaky vaccine, where 1-IRR underestimates the per-exposure parameter; that does not apply here.)

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing vaccine (fraction \(p\) of recipients fully protected, fraction \(1-p\) unaffected), the hazard/incidence rate among vaccinated individuals is constantly scaled by exactly \(1-p\) relative to unvaccinated individuals (assuming identical exposure). Thus 1-IRR recovers \(p\) exactly. This matches the average per-exposure efficacy (100% for the protected fraction, 0% otherwise), so the estimator is unbiased. (Contrast with cumulative incidence ratios, which can differ under repeated exposures.)

8.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing vaccine, a fixed fraction \(\epsilon\) of vaccinated individuals are fully protected (infection probability per exposure drops to 0) while the remainder have the same per-exposure infection probability \(p\) as unvaccinated individuals. Exposures occur as a Poisson process at the same rate in both arms. The observed incidence rate (cases per person-time) among the vaccinated is therefore exactly \((1-\epsilon)\) times the unvaccinated incidence rate at every instant, because only the unprotected fraction contributes cases while every participant contributes person-time. Consequently the incidence rate ratio equals \(1-\epsilon\) constantly, so \(1-\text{IRR}=\epsilon\) recovers the per-exposure vaccine efficacy without bias. (The same algebra holds for a leaky vaccine under constant hazards; bias appears only when cumulative incidence rather than rates is used, owing to differential depletion of susceptibles.)

C. correctly estimate

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fixed fraction p of recipients are fully protected (efficacy = 1 per exposure) while the remainder are completely unprotected. Under a constant force of infection the observed incidence rate in the vaccinated arm is therefore exactly (1 – p) times the rate in the unvaccinated arm, so IRR = 1 – p and 1 – IRR recovers p exactly. Because the per-exposure efficacy is also p (the weighted average of 1 and 0), the 1-IRR estimator is unbiased for the per-exposure quantity. (The same algebra does not hold for leaky vaccines, but that is outside the scope of the question.)

Thus the correct choice is C. correctly estimate.

An all-or-nothing vaccine confers complete protection to a fixed fraction \(p\) of recipients and zero protection to the remainder.  

Under a constant exposure (hazard) process, the vaccinated cohort therefore experiences an instantaneous hazard equal to \((1-p)\lambda\). The observed incidence rate (cases per person-time) in the vaccinated arm is accordingly scaled by exactly \((1-p)\) relative to the unvaccinated arm. Consequently the quantity \(1-\text{IRR}\) recovers \(p\) directly, which is also the average per-exposure efficacy across the cohort. (Time-varying hazards induced by differential depletion do not alter the algebraic identity when incidence rates are computed from the observed person-time denominators.)  

Thus 1-IRR correctly estimates per-exposure VE for an all-or-nothing vaccine.  

Final answer: C
